One of the things I got that completely surprised me how well the setup worked was a deep freeze. This one is a stand-up model and I came across it cheap. What's so surprising is that what it does while keeping bottled water in it. The expiration date on bottled water is for the plastic so you want to keep it cool and dark because it keeps longer. It doesn't get much cooler and darker than in a freezer. I figure that if the plastic starts to break down while it's frozen, I can always cut open a bottle or two and use it to rinse off the rest of the ice (prevents plastic leeching into the water).

I recently bought a house so I knew that I would need to move it so I unplugged it.

@totes_magotes is right, Sawyer Mini on the water filtration. Here's what I would recommend absent one of those. First, get a cooling towel. It's just a shammy but this sumbitch works. If your area becomes unsafe, having this for a bugout option is great. You can use it to drape over your head or around your neck but it also works as a water filter. Water passes through it and any debris doesn't. Best part about the cooling towel is that it washes off easily and then you slap that sucker right back into the container wet and you still have a cooling towel on hand. That's good for filtration but let's talk purification.

A Klean Kanteen 40 oz bottle. Single Wall, Stainless steel. Filtered water from a bag, strained through the cooling towel and into the bottle. Get a fish mouth spreader and use it to either suspend the bottle above a fire or stick the thing into a fire to boil the water. Once the water is boiled, carefully remove it and let it cool before putting the cap back onto it. Slide the entire thing into one of those Condor Tactical Bottle holders with your fish mouth spreader and you have a ready supply of water to drink for later. You can use that to fill a separate plastic canteen if you like. There's another pouch in the bottle holder, use this fucker to store one of those UST Pocket stoves that basically clones the design of an Esbit stove and it comes with firestarting tabs.

Anyone Can Survive For Only...

3 seconds without hope (your prepping completely takes care of this one) 3 minutes without air 3 hours without adequate shelter in harsh conditions 3 days without water and 3 weeks without food.

Container (something to boil and store water in)

Cutting tool (I'd take a couple of these at least)

Cordage (Bankline or Paracord)

Combustion (You need to make fire)

Cover (Something that you can use to shelter yourself from the elements)

The biggest thing is that knowledge is the best prep. If you know enough, you can trim your gear down drastically. It's cool to have all this gear to help you survive but it doesn't do you any good if you really can't carry it however-many-mile you need to go on foot to your location should you find yourself in that situation. Probably the best thing I can recommend is to talk to some hikers who do the long trails like the Appalachian Trail. They do stuff like cut most of the handle off of a toothbrush, use a bandana instead of a washrag or toilet paper, etc etc. Most of the time, they're looking at mid 20 pounds for their gear weight and I think that that's a reasonable amount. It's better to get to your stopping point with enough energy to prep your camp and eat than to get there dead beat and tired.

I have to go with Totes again on the cutting down on the gear bit. At present, I've got an INCH bag that is pretty damned heavy and I'm looking to cut unnecessary gear from it. I'm still learning all the time, though so, eventually, some of that might just get busted down into smaller packs and I might even be able to turn one into a full car kit

Consider a modular approach with molle webbing. Configurable and quick to ditch or add stuff. You can have a base pack for bugging out, a module for first aid, a module for INCH, etc. even a module for "I can ditch this if it's too heavy or I need to really move fast."

I also always recommend a kindle or similar to cut down on book weight.

Instead of carrying full meals, learn how to forage and hunt but carry small packs with fats in them (to avoid protein starvation). Things like that.
